prompt:
On May 4, 2026, you are advising ArchiveFox, a 16-person B2B SaaS company that manages collections workflows for 31 museums. It has $1.7 million ARR and 20 months of runway. The CEO still approves every implementation exception: go-live sequencing, data-mapping deviations, service credits, and any unusual customer promise.

From January 1 through March 31, the implementation tracker recorded 48 exception requests. Twenty waited more than two business days for a decision (median 3.4 days); nine delayed a go-live, and six produced contradictory dates because Implementation and Customer Success each thought the other would decide. Fifteen of the twenty delayed requests were routine sequencing or mapping choices matching patterns accepted before. Four involved new security or contract terms and were promptly sent to the existing security adviser or counsel; one has no usable record. Once the CEO answered, the team completed 17 of the 20 without overtime or added staff. One delay moved the start of $42,000 in annual recurring revenue by three weeks.

In an April 6–17 shadow exercise, the Head of Implementation wrote down a decision before the CEO in 18 cases. The CEO later chose the same action in 16. The two differences were a credit above $8,000 and an unsupported data-retention promise. No customer was affected by the exercise. Implementation utilization averaged 69%, and post-decision backlog stayed near 1.2 days.

The CEO says delegation could make promises spiral. The Head of Implementation says routine calls are manageable but the limits are unclear. Customer Success wants a reliable escalation clock. An investor recommends hiring a COO now and adding a weekly cross-functional approval council because the company may reach 25 people next year; there is no role charter or costed capacity model. A twice-daily CEO Slack queue tried in March did not reduce waits, and the CEO expects to remain unavailable about ten hours each week.

Write a concise decision memo, dated May 4, 2026 and no longer than 1,500 words. Recommend what ArchiveFox should do now, what it should explicitly defer or reject, how to operate for the next six weeks, and how leadership will decide what happens afterward. Preserve customer continuity, state material caveats, and do not assume facts not provided.
criteria: Pass only if the memo makes the recurring routine-decision queue and ambiguous authority the primary organizational problem and selects a decision-rights intervention (the exact label is unnecessary), while explicitly rejecting or deferring the COO hire, approval council or new layer, and broad reorganization because the evidence does not show a residual capability or capacity gap; otherwise fail.

Pass only if the diagnosis explicitly separates decision-material observations, claims, and unknowns (those labels or clear semantic equivalents), treats the tracker, shadow exercise, utilization, and runway data as observations, the CEO, team, and investor statements as claims, and delegation sustainability, causal attribution, exception-boundary quality, and future effects as unknown rather than proved, and names at least one causal rival; otherwise fail.

Pass only if the proposed operating design names one accountable end-to-end implementation or go-live outcome owner and specifies routine decision domains and numeric or directly observable limits, required consultation or review, notification, an escalation trigger with destination and deadline, at least one interface service expectation, backup or absence coverage, an audit artifact, and customer-continuity ownership, while retaining qualified review for security and contract exceptions; otherwise fail.

Pass only if the memo proposes a time-bounded reversible pilot with named change and evidence owners, start, intermediate, and final dates (dates derivable from May 4 are acceptable), affected scope, baseline and artifacts, numeric or directly observable outcome and harm measures, and safeguards for customer continuity, unauthorized commitments, security and contract review, rollback, and evidence preservation; otherwise fail.

Pass only if the closure states the decision now, unresolved unknowns, preserved prior-state option, and switch condition, and gives measurable end-of-pilot thresholds for four distinct results: keep the current pilot scope, revise exactly one boundary, interface, measure, or workload assumption once, add capacity only if a sustained residual gap remains after decision and interface causes are addressed and exceeds full role cost, and roll back or stop on a harm limit; each result must name its next owner and action, otherwise fail.
